listitem.autoauthsectiontext: Hospital admission is/was needed for appropriate care of the patient because of
listitem.para: Admission is indicated for 1 or more of the following:
Osteomyelitis diagnosed or cannot be excluded in observation care (ie, empiric course of treatment with parenteral antibiotics planned) and 1 or more of the following:

Presentation is consistent with acute osteomyelitis (ie, not chronic osteomyelitis such as diabetic foot or relapse of previously treated osteomyelitis).
If acute osteomyelitis is diagnosed, or cannot be excluded in observation care (empiric treatment planned), a course of parenteral antibiotics is indicated, with care provided initially in the inpatient setting. These patients should be closely monitored and may require additional urgent medical or surgical treatment initially or within the first few days of treatment (eg, surgical debridement or drainage, management of hypotension, altered mental status, adjustment of antibiotics).
Chronic osteomyelitis is defined as a more protracted, often indolent disease process that is often a relapse of infection in the same site weeks to years after treatment of the initial infection. Chronic osteomyelitis is usually polymicrobial and generally cannot be eradicated without surgical treatment. Diabetic foot and posttraumatic osteomyelitis are examples of infections that can become chronic. Common features of chronic osteomyelitis are the presence of dead bone (sequestrum) or involucrum (reactive bony encasement of the sequestrum) and sinus tracts if there is extension through cortical bone.

guideline-sect3.heading: Extended Stay
guideline-sect3.para: Minimal (a few hours to 1 day), Brief (1 to 3 days), Moderate (4 to 7 days), and Prolonged (more than 7 days).

listitem.para: Extended stay beyond goal length of stay may be needed for:
Failure to meet discharge criteria (recovery milestones within final day in Optimal Recovery Course)
Expect brief stay extension.
Inadequate clinical response to antibiotics (eg, continued fever, hypotension)
Anticipate continued parenteral antibiotics, repeat cultures to confirm bacterial etiology and sensitivity of bacteria to antibiotics, and evaluation for other possible fever etiologies.
Expect brief to moderate stay extension.
Anticipate repeat blood cultures until confirmed no growth.
Expect brief stay extension.
Surgical intervention needed (eg, beyond superficial debridement)
Surgical intervention may include drainage procedure, fracture fixation, removal of prosthetic device, vascular restoration, excision for osteonecrosis, or amputation.
Bony defects left after debridement may require surgical replacement with tissue or bone grafts, or with antibiotic-impregnated spacers.
External fixation devices may be required.
Expect brief to moderate stay extension.
Vertebral osteomyelitis with spinal cord compression, abscess formation, or mechanical instability
Epidural and subdural abscesses may require drainage.
Anticipate possible surgical debridement or corpectomy.
Expect brief to moderate stay extension.
Antibiotic-resistant organism identified (eg, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus)
Expect brief stay extension.
Severe concomitant cellulitis (eg, overlaying ulcer infection) or pressure injury (eg, stage 3 or stage 4)
Anticipate wound care (eg, debridement, dressings) and clinical reassessment.
Expect brief stay extension.
Acute metabolic disorder (eg, acidosis, hyponatremia, hypernatremia) not rapidly responsive to treatment
Anticipate adjustment of medication, fluid administration, and follow-up laboratory testing.
Expect brief stay extension.
Clinically significant malnutrition (eg, BMI less than 18.5, loss of subcutaneous fat (eg, orbital, triceps, over ribs), loss of muscle mass (eg, temples, clavicles, hands))BMI Calculator
Anticipate nutritional assessments and supplementation.
Expect brief stay extension.
Acute kidney injury (stage 2), Acute renal failure (stage 3 acute kidney injury), or severe chronic renal disease (eg, GFR less than 30 mL/min/1.73m2 (0.5 mL/sec/1.73m2))eGFR - Adult Calculator
Anticipate adjustment of medication and follow-up laboratory testing.
Expect brief stay extension.
Unstable comorbidities (eg, heart failure)
Anticipate treatment of specific comorbidity.
Expect brief stay extension.

guideline-sect3.heading: Background
guideline-sect3.para: Patients with acute osteomyelitis often present with fever, rigors, and may even appear toxic. Patients with acute osteomyelitis are hospitalized for IV antibiotic treatment and some will also need operative debridement. Depending on the location of osteomyelitis, local extension of an invasive suppurative process can lead to septic arthritis, brain abscess, meningitis, spinal cord compression, pneumonia, and empyema.

Hematogenous spread of bacteria causes almost all cases of osteomyelitis in children; in adults, it usually presents as vertebral osteomyelitis. Medical management with antibiotics may be sufficient for hematogenous osteomyelitis. For other types of osteomyelitis, including contiguous focus osteomyelitis (eg, cellulitis, septic arthritis, or other infection progressing to infect contiguous bone), posttraumatic osteomyelitis (eg, subsequent to an open fracture), and prosthetic implant-related infection, definitive care often necessitates surgery in addition to parenteral antibiotics.

Chronic osteomyelitis is defined as a more protracted, often indolent disease process that is often a relapse of infection in the same site weeks to years after treatment of the initial infection. Chronic osteomyelitis is usually polymicrobial and generally cannot be eradicated without surgical treatment. Diabetic foot and posttraumatic osteomyelitis are examples of infections that can become chronic. Common features of chronic osteomyelitis are the presence of dead bone (sequestrum) or involucrum (reactive bony encasement of the sequestrum) and sinus tracts if there is extension through cortical bone.

guideline-sect3.heading: Criteria
guideline-sect3.para: The evidence for the clinical indications found in this guideline includes 10 published peer reviewed articles, 1 specialty society or other evidence-based guideline, and 2 book sections.

Analysis of an all-payer database shows a mean length of stay of 8.1 days for patients admitted to inpatient care. A consensus guideline states that admission to inpatient care is appropriate for patients who have severe limb-threatening infections.

guideline-sect3.heading: Alternatives
guideline-sect3.para: The principal role of observation care in terms of acute osteomyelitis (ie, not chronic osteomyelitis such as diabetic foot or relapse of previously treated osteomyelitis) is to afford time beyond emergency department care to confirm the diagnosis.

guideline-sect3.heading: Hospitalization
guideline-sect3.para: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 randomized controlled trials including 1321 adult patients with osteomyelitis found that therapy with a major oral antibiotic component to therapy was noninferior when compared with IV treatment alone.

guideline-sect3.heading: Length of Stay
guideline-sect3.para: Analysis of national hospital discharge data for an adult population shows 29% of hospitalized patients with the principal diagnosis of osteomyelitis were discharged in 3 days or less.

guideline-sect3.heading: Rationale
guideline-sect3.para: Use of this MCG care guideline helps the clinician identify patient-specific complex clinical factors that make it reasonable to expect a necessity for hospital care across 2 or more midnights. The evidence-based clinical criteria assist the clinician in the decision to appropriately admit a patient to inpatient care. For Medicare enrollees, MCG care guidelines also support the clinician in the decision to appropriately admit a patient to inpatient care when there is not an expectation of 2 or more midnights of hospital care (eg, CMS' Two-Midnight Rule exceptions).

Use of these evidence-based clinical criteria to support decision making around the need for inpatient treatment is of clinical benefit to the patient and is crucial for quality patient care. Use of evidence-based clinical criteria ensures patients receive the most appropriate care for their specific condition, reduces unnecessary risks, promotes recovery, and provides a standard that can reduce disparities in care. Evidence-based clinical criteria not only help align treatment decisions with best practice, but they can also help reduce unwarranted variation in care by fostering consistency and equality in healthcare provision across regions and facilities. Appropriate use of the evidence-based clinical criteria in conjunction with the Supplemental Medicare Criteria ensures Medicare patients receive full access to Medicare benefits (eg, inpatient care), without risk of delay or decreased access, based on variables such as clinical severity of illness, length of provision of medically necessary hospital-level care, or satisfaction of specified Medicare criteria as directed by CMS. Use of these criteria will help ensure that the patient receives necessary care in the appropriate setting.

guideline-sect3.heading: Related CMS Coverage Guidance
guideline-sect3.para: This guideline supplements but does not replace, modify, or supersede existing Medicare regulations or applicable National Coverage Determinations (NCDs) or Local Coverage Determinations (LCDs).
